focus: Exodus 8 continues the plagues with frogs, lice, and swarms of flies, each pressing Pharaoh with the LORD’s demand, “Let My people go, that they may serve Me” (Exodus 8:1). The chapter traces a pattern of temporary relief followed by renewed hardness, while the magicians reach the end of their power and the LORD begins to set His people apart from Egypt.

sections.title: Frogs Cover the Land and Pharaoh Breaks His Word
sections.summary: Frogs come up from the waters and fill Egypt’s houses, and Pharaoh begs Moses to entreat the LORD, promising to let the people go. Moses lets Pharaoh choose the time so that he may know “that there is no one like the LORD our God” (Exodus 8:10), but when Pharaoh sees relief, he hardens his heart.

sections.title: The Dust Becomes Lice and the Magicians Confess God’s Finger
sections.summary: Aaron strikes the dust and it becomes lice on man and beast throughout Egypt, and the magicians cannot reproduce the sign. They tell Pharaoh, “This is the finger of God” (Exodus 8:19), yet Pharaoh’s heart grows hard, as the LORD had said.

sections.title: Swarms of Flies Strike Egypt but Spare Goshen
sections.summary: The LORD sends swarms of flies on Egypt but sets apart the land of Goshen, “that you may know that I am the LORD in the midst of the land” (Exodus 8:22). Pharaoh offers to let Israel sacrifice in the land and then only a short distance away, Moses insists on the three days’ journey God commands, and once the flies are removed, Pharaoh hardens his heart again.

1.brief: The LORD sends Moses to Pharaoh with the word, “Let My people go, that they may serve Me.” The demand is renewed before the second plague.
1.explain:
“And the LORD spoke to Moses, ‘Go to Pharaoh and say to him, ‘Thus says the LORD:”

After the plague of blood, God sends Moses back to Pharaoh with His word.

“Let My people go, that they may serve Me.”

The demand is renewed before the second plague. God’s claim has not changed. Israel belongs to Him and must be free to “serve” Him.
1.notes: In Hebrew Bibles, the first four verses of this chapter are counted as the last four verses of chapter 7, so the rest of chapter 8 is numbered four verses lower. The NKJV follows the English numbering.

2.brief: If Pharaoh refuses, the LORD will strike all his territory with frogs. The warning gives Pharaoh a choice before judgment falls.
2.explain:
“But if you refuse to let them go,”

God gives Pharaoh a choice. If he refuses, judgment will follow.

“behold, I will smite all your territory with frogs.”

God will strike “all your territory with frogs.” Frogs were common along the Nile, especially after the yearly flood. But this would be a plague beyond anything normal. The warning gives Pharaoh a choice before judgment falls.

3.brief: The river will bring forth frogs that will come into Pharaoh’s house, bedroom, and bed, and into his servants’ houses, ovens, and kneading bowls. The plague will invade every part of Egyptian life, from the palace to the kitchen.
3.explain:
“So the river shall bring forth frogs abundantly,”

The river that had just turned to blood will now “bring forth frogs abundantly.” The Hebrew word suggests swarming, the same word used for Israel’s growth in 1:7.

“which shall go up and come into your house, into your bedroom, on your bed,”

The frogs will invade Pharaoh’s private spaces: “your house,” “your bedroom,” even “your bed.” The king who thought himself untouchable will find no place to escape.

“into the houses of your servants, on your people, into your ovens, and into your kneading bowls.”

The plague will reach everyone, from the palace to the kitchen. Frogs will be in the “ovens,” where bread was baked, and in the “kneading bowls,” where dough was prepared. The plague will invade every part of Egyptian life.
3.notes: The Hebrew verb behind “shall bring forth frogs abundantly” is the verb for swarming used in Genesis 1:20–21 and Exodus 1:7.

4.brief: The frogs will come up on Pharaoh, his people, and all his servants. The threat is aimed at Pharaoh and the whole Egyptian court and nation.
4.explain:
“And the frogs shall come up on you, on your people, and on all your servants.”

The frogs will climb “on you,” on Pharaoh himself. The threat is aimed at Pharaoh and the whole Egyptian court and nation.

5.brief: The LORD tells Moses to have Aaron stretch out his rod over the waters to bring frogs on the land. The plague comes at God’s direction through the rod.
5.explain:
“Then the LORD spoke to Moses, ‘Say to Aaron, ‘Stretch out your hand with your rod over the streams, over the rivers, and over the ponds,”

Aaron is to stretch out the rod over every source of water, the same places struck in the first plague (7:19).

“and cause frogs to come up on the land of Egypt.”

The plague comes at God’s direction through the rod.

6.brief: Aaron stretches out his hand, and frogs come up and cover the land of Egypt. God’s word is fulfilled immediately.
6.explain:
“So Aaron stretched out his hand over the waters of Egypt, and the frogs came up and covered the land of Egypt.”

Aaron obeyed, and the frogs “covered the land.” God’s word was fulfilled immediately.
6.notes: The Hebrew word for “frogs” is singular in this verse, used as a collective noun for a mass of frogs.

7.brief: The magicians do the same with their enchantments and bring frogs on the land. Their imitation only adds to Egypt’s trouble rather than removing it.
7.explain:
“And the magicians did so with their enchantments, and brought up frogs on the land of Egypt.”

The magicians imitated the plague. They “brought up frogs.” Their imitation only added to Egypt’s trouble. Yet Pharaoh did not look to them for relief. He called for Moses and Aaron and asked them to entreat the LORD to take the frogs away (8:8), and when Moses cried out to the LORD, the frogs died (8:12–13).

8.brief: Pharaoh calls Moses and Aaron and asks them to “Entreat the LORD” to take away the frogs, promising to let the people go to sacrifice. For the first time Pharaoh asks for the LORD’s help and promises to obey.
8.explain:
“Then Pharaoh called for Moses and Aaron, and said, ‘Entreat the LORD that He may take away the frogs from me and from my people;”

For the first time, Pharaoh asks for help. He asks Moses and Aaron to “Entreat the LORD,” to pray to Him. The king who said, “Who is the LORD?” (5:2) now uses His name and asks for His help.

“and I will let the people go, that they may sacrifice to the LORD.”

Pharaoh makes a promise: he “will let the people go.” For the first time Pharaoh asks for the LORD’s help and promises to obey.

9.brief: Moses gives Pharaoh the honor of choosing when he should pray for the frogs to be destroyed. Letting Pharaoh set the time will make it clear that the relief comes from God.
9.explain:
“And Moses said to Pharaoh, ‘Accept the honor of saying when I shall intercede for you,”

Moses gives Pharaoh the right to choose when Moses will pray. Moses offers Pharaoh control over the timing so that no one could say the frogs left by chance.

“for your servants, and for your people, to destroy the frogs from you and your houses, that they may remain in the river only.”

The frogs will be removed from the land and will “remain in the river only.” Letting Pharaoh set the time will make it clear that the relief comes from God.
9.notes: The Hebrew phrase translated “Accept the honor” is unusual. It may mean literally have the glory over me, an invitation to Pharaoh to set the terms.

10.brief: Pharaoh says, “Tomorrow,” and Moses agrees, “that you may know that there is no one like the LORD our God.” The timing will prove the LORD’s unique power.
10.explain:
“So he said, ‘Tomorrow.”

Pharaoh chose “Tomorrow.” Why he did not ask for immediate relief is not stated. He may have hoped the frogs would leave on their own.

“And he said, ‘Let it be according to your word, that you may know that there is no one like the LORD our God.”

Moses agrees. The frogs will leave exactly when Pharaoh asked, so that he may know “there is no one like the LORD our God.” The timing will prove the LORD’s unique power.

11.brief: Moses promises that the frogs will leave Pharaoh, his houses, his servants, and his people and remain only in the river. God’s relief will be as complete as the plague.
11.explain:
“And the frogs shall depart from you, from your houses, from your servants, and from your people.”

Moses promises that the frogs will leave every place they invaded.

“They shall remain in the river only.”

They will return to the river, where frogs belong. God’s relief will be as complete as the plague.

12.brief: Moses and Aaron leave Pharaoh, and Moses cries out to the LORD concerning the frogs. Moses intercedes for the king who oppresses Israel.
12.explain:
“Then Moses and Aaron went out from Pharaoh.”

The brothers leave the palace.

“And Moses cried out to the LORD concerning the frogs which He had brought against Pharaoh.”

Moses “cried out to the LORD.” He prays earnestly. The narrator notes that God “had brought” the frogs. The same God who sent them will remove them. Moses intercedes for the king who oppresses Israel.

13.brief: The LORD does according to Moses’ word, and the frogs die in the houses, courtyards, and fields. God answers Moses’ prayer exactly.
13.explain:
“So the LORD did according to the word of Moses.”

God answered Moses’ prayer. He acted “according to the word of Moses.”

“And the frogs died out of the houses, out of the courtyards, and out of the fields.”

The frogs “died” everywhere: in “the houses,” “the courtyards,” and “the fields.” God answers Moses’ prayer exactly.

14.brief: The Egyptians gather the frogs into heaps, and the land stinks. Even the relief leaves a reminder of the judgment.
14.explain:
“They gathered them together in heaps, and the land stank.”

The Egyptians piled the dead frogs “in heaps,” and “the land stank.” Even the relief left a reminder of the judgment.
14.notes: The Hebrew phrase translated “in heaps” repeats the word for “heap,” literally heaps, heaps, emphasizing the great number.

15.brief: “But when Pharaoh saw that there was relief, he hardened his heart” and did not heed them, as the LORD had said. Pharaoh breaks his promise as soon as the pressure lifts.
15.explain:
“But when Pharaoh saw that there was relief, he hardened his heart”

“But” marks the turn. As soon as Pharaoh saw “relief,” he “hardened his heart.” Here the text says plainly that Pharaoh hardened his own heart. Pressure brought a promise. Relief brought a broken promise.

“and did not heed them, as the LORD had said.”

Pharaoh did not keep his word. This happened “as the LORD had said.” Pharaoh broke his promise as soon as the pressure lifted. His actions after relief showed what his earlier promise was worth.
15.notes:
The Hebrew verb translated “hardened” here means to make heavy, the same root as in 7:14. Pharaoh made his own heart heavy and unresponsive.

The Hebrew word translated “relief” means breathing room or respite.

16.brief: The LORD tells Moses to have Aaron strike the dust so that it becomes lice throughout Egypt. The third plague comes without warning to Pharaoh.
16.explain:
“So the LORD said to Moses, ‘Say to Aaron, ‘Stretch out your rod, and strike the dust of the land,”

The third plague comes without warning. God sends no message to Pharaoh first. Pharaoh had broken his word, and the next judgment falls immediately.

“so that it may become lice throughout all the land of Egypt.”

The “dust” will become “lice.” Egypt’s very soil will be turned against its people.
16.notes: The Hebrew word translated “lice” may refer to gnats, mosquitoes, or lice. Its exact meaning is uncertain.

17.brief: Aaron strikes the dust, and it becomes lice on man and beast throughout all the land. Egypt’s very soil is turned against its people.
17.explain:
“And they did so. For Aaron stretched out his hand with his rod and struck the dust of the earth,”

Aaron obeyed. He struck “the dust of the earth.”

“and it became lice on man and beast. All the dust of the land became lice throughout all the land of Egypt.”

The plague affected “man and beast.” “All the dust” became lice. The repetition stresses that the plague was total. Egypt’s very soil was turned against its people.

18.brief: The magicians try to bring forth lice with their enchantments, “but they could not.” Egypt’s power now reaches its limit.
18.explain:
“Now the magicians so worked with their enchantments to bring forth lice,”

The magicians tried to do the same thing.

“but they could not.”

Egypt’s power reached its limit. For the first time, the magicians failed.

“So there were lice on man and beast.”

The lice remained on people and animals. Egypt had no answer.

19.brief: The magicians tell Pharaoh, “This is the finger of God,” yet Pharaoh’s heart grows hard, and he does not heed them, as the LORD had said. Even Pharaoh’s own experts recognize God’s hand, but Pharaoh refuses to listen.
19.explain:
“Then the magicians said to Pharaoh, ‘This is the finger of God.”

The magicians admitted defeat. “This is the finger of God.” They recognized that this plague came from a power beyond anything they could match. “Finger of God” describes God’s direct action. The same phrase describes how the tablets of the law were written (31:18), and Jesus used it of His power over demons (Luke 11:20).

“But Pharaoh’s heart grew hard, and he did not heed them, just as the LORD had said.”

Pharaoh would not listen even to his own experts. His heart “grew hard.” Even Pharaoh’s own experts recognized God’s hand, but Pharaoh refused to listen.
19.notes: The magicians speak of “God” rather than “the LORD.” They recognize divine power without confessing the LORD as Israel’s God.

20.brief: The LORD tells Moses to rise early and meet Pharaoh at the water with the word, “Let My people go, that they may serve Me.” The fourth plague begins with a fresh warning.
20.explain:
“And the LORD said to Moses, ‘Rise early in the morning and stand before Pharaoh as he comes out to the water.”

God sends Moses to meet Pharaoh at the water again, as before the first plague (7:15).

“Then say to him, ‘Thus says the LORD: ‘Let My people go, that they may serve Me.”

The demand is repeated. The fourth plague begins with a fresh warning.

21.brief: If Pharaoh refuses, God will send swarms of flies on him, his servants, his people, and their houses. The judgment will fill Egypt’s homes and land.
21.explain:
“Or else, if you will not let My people go, behold, I will send swarms of flies on you and your servants, on your people and into your houses.”

If Pharaoh refuses, God will send “swarms of flies.” They will fill everything: Pharaoh, his servants, his people, and their houses.

“The houses of the Egyptians shall be full of swarms of flies, and also the ground on which they stand.”

The flies will cover even “the ground on which they stand.” The judgment will fill Egypt’s homes and land.
21.notes: The Hebrew word translated “swarms of flies” refers to a mixture or swarm. Its exact meaning is uncertain. Some take it to mean flies of various kinds, others a particular biting fly.

22.brief: God will set apart the land of Goshen where Israel lives, so that no flies will be there, “in order that you may know that I am the LORD in the midst of the land.” For the first time God openly distinguishes Israel’s land from Egypt’s.
22.explain:
“And in that day I will set apart the land of Goshen, in which My people dwell,”

For the first time, God openly distinguishes Israel’s land from Egypt’s. He will “set apart the land of Goshen,” the region where Israel lived (Genesis 47:27).

“that no swarms of flies shall be there,”

There will be no flies in Goshen. Israel will be spared.

“in order that you may know that I am the LORD in the midst of the land.”

The purpose: Pharaoh will “know that I am the LORD in the midst of the land.” The LORD is not a distant God limited to Israel’s land. He is present and active in Egypt itself. He knows His people and protects them, even in the land of their oppressors.
22.notes: The Hebrew verb translated “set apart” means to make a distinction. God’s distinction between Israel and Egypt appears again in 9:4, 9:26, 10:23, and 11:7.

23.brief: God says, “I will make a difference between My people and your people,” and sets the sign for tomorrow. The plague will show that the LORD knows and protects His own.
23.explain:
“I will make a difference between My people and your people.”

God says He “will make a difference” between His people and Pharaoh’s people. The plague will show that the LORD knows and protects His own.

“Tomorrow this sign shall be.”

God sets the time: “Tomorrow.” As with the frogs, the timing will show that the plague comes from God.
23.notes: The Hebrew word translated “a difference” is unusual. It usually means redemption or ransom. The Greek translation reads “a distinction.” God’s distinction of Israel already points toward their redemption.

24.brief: The LORD does so, and thick swarms of flies come into Pharaoh’s house, his servants’ houses, and all Egypt, corrupting the land. God’s warning is fulfilled in full.
24.explain:
“And the LORD did so.”

God did exactly what He said.

“Thick swarms of flies came into the house of Pharaoh, into his servants’ houses, and into all the land of Egypt.”

“Thick swarms” filled Pharaoh’s palace, his officials’ houses, and the whole land.

“The land was corrupted because of the swarms of flies.”

The land “was corrupted,” ruined. God’s warning was fulfilled in full.

25.brief: Pharaoh calls Moses and Aaron and says, “Go, sacrifice to your God in the land.” He offers worship on his own terms, inside Egypt.
25.explain:
“Then Pharaoh called for Moses and Aaron, and said, ‘Go, sacrifice to your God in the land.”

Pharaoh makes his first offer. Israel may sacrifice, but only “in the land,” inside Egypt. He offers worship on his own terms. He will allow Israel to worship as long as they stay under his control.

26.brief: Moses answers that it would not be right, because their sacrifices would be an abomination to the Egyptians, who might stone them for offering such sacrifices before their eyes. Worship inside Egypt would put Israel in danger.
26.explain:
“And Moses said, ‘It is not right to do so,”

Moses refuses Pharaoh’s terms. “It is not right.”

“for we would be sacrificing the abomination of the Egyptians to the LORD our God.”

Moses explains that Israel’s sacrifices would be “the abomination of the Egyptians,” something the Egyptians found offensive. Moses does not say exactly what would offend them, but sacrifices that were right before the LORD would be detestable in Egyptian eyes.

“If we sacrifice the abomination of the Egyptians before their eyes, then will they not stone us?”

If Israel offered such sacrifices in Egypt, the Egyptians might “stone” them. Worship inside Egypt would put Israel in danger.
26.notes: Genesis 46:34 says that “every shepherd is an abomination to the Egyptians.” The exact reason Israel’s sacrifices would offend the Egyptians is not stated.

27.brief: Moses insists that they will go three days’ journey into the wilderness and sacrifice “as He will command us.” The LORD, not Pharaoh, sets the terms of Israel’s worship.
27.explain:
“We will go three days’ journey into the wilderness and sacrifice to the LORD our God”

Moses repeats God’s original request (3:18). Israel must go “into the wilderness.”

“as He will command us.”

God would give the instructions for the sacrifice. The LORD, not Pharaoh, sets the terms of Israel’s worship. Israel cannot worship God on Pharaoh’s terms.

28.brief: Pharaoh agrees to let them go into the wilderness, “only you shall not go very far away,” and asks Moses to intercede for him. He gives way only partly and still tries to keep Israel within reach.
28.explain:
“So Pharaoh said, ‘I will let you go, that you may sacrifice to the LORD your God in the wilderness;”

Pharaoh appears to give in. He “will let you go” into “the wilderness.”

“only you shall not go very far away.”

But he adds a condition. He wants to keep Israel within reach. He gives way only partly.

“Intercede for me.”

Pharaoh asks Moses to pray for him. He wants relief without real surrender.

29.brief: Moses promises to pray that the flies depart tomorrow but warns Pharaoh not to “deal deceitfully anymore” in refusing to let the people go. Moses calls Pharaoh’s earlier broken promise what it was.
29.explain:
“Then Moses said, ‘Indeed I am going out from you, and I will entreat the LORD,”

Moses agrees to pray.

“that the swarms of flies may depart tomorrow from Pharaoh, from his servants, and from his people.”

Moses promises that the flies will leave “tomorrow.”

“But let Pharaoh not deal deceitfully anymore in not letting the people go to sacrifice to the LORD.”

Moses adds a warning. Pharaoh must “not deal deceitfully anymore.” Moses names Pharaoh’s earlier broken promise for what it was: deceit (8:15).

30.brief: Moses goes out from Pharaoh and entreats the LORD. Once again Moses prays for the man who opposes him.
30.explain:
“So Moses went out from Pharaoh and entreated the LORD.”

Moses prayed for Pharaoh again. Once again Moses prays for the man who opposes him.

31.brief: The LORD does as Moses asked and removes the flies, so that “Not one remained.” God’s relief is complete.
31.explain:
“And the LORD did according to the word of Moses;”

God answered Moses’ prayer.

“He removed the swarms of flies from Pharaoh, from his servants, and from his people. Not one remained.”

The flies were completely removed. “Not one remained.” God’s relief was complete.

32.brief: “But Pharaoh hardened his heart at this time also” and did not let the people go. Pharaoh repeats the pattern of the frogs and breaks his word again.
32.explain:
“But Pharaoh hardened his heart at this time also;”

“But” again marks the turn. Pharaoh “hardened his heart at this time also,” just as he did after the frogs (8:15). The text says again that Pharaoh did this himself.

“neither would he let the people go.”

Pharaoh broke his word again. He repeated the pattern of the frogs. Relief from judgment did not soften him. It hardened him further.
